intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene (139312) on chromosome 18p11.21.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia. It is mainly cervical, and age at onset ranges widely. Onset is usually in the neck. Dystonia often spreads to other sites, especially the cranial and facial muscles, and speech is commonly involved. Arm involvement is less frequent, and some patients develop generalized dystonia (Fuchs et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected. Mean age at onset was 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7 affected individuals the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) described 28 individuals with definite dystonia from 8 multiplex families with GNAL mutations. All were Caucasian of mixed European ancestry. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82%, and 93% had neck involvement at final examination. However, most patients progressed to other sites, and only 46% had focal dystonia at last examination. Cranial involvement was present in 57% and speech involvement in 44%. Brachial onset was not observed, and only 32% had arm involvement. The authors noted that these features distinguished the disorder from DYT6. Fuchs et al. (2013) summarized the phenotype as mainly cervical dystonia with a relatively broad range of age at onset. In over half of subjects the dystonia spread to other muscles, especially facial muscles. Some individuals had generalized dystonia with onset in the leg, and other onset sites included the larynx, jaw, and tongue.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in 2 families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia and found heterozygous GNAL mutations in both. Family P carried a nonsense mutation (S293X), which lay within 1 of 3 regions of potential linkage (lod scores 1.5 to 2.1). Family D1 carried a missense mutation (V137M). The authors then Sanger sequenced the GNAL coding region in 39 additional multiplex families of mixed European origin who were negative for DYT1 and DYT6 mutations. They found 6 additional novel mutations in 6 families (19%). These included 2 frameshift insertions, 1 nonsense mutation, 1 missense mutation, a 9-bp in-frame deletion, and a possible splice site mutation. In every family with DNA from multiple affected individuals, the mutation segregated with the disease. None of the variants was found in dbSNP135, about 3,500 European exomes, or 572 control chromosomes.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) tested mutant proteins in a cell-based BRET assay in HEK293 cells. The assay measured Galpha-olf function through its interaction with Gbeta-gamma subunits during the D1 dopamine receptor (D1R)-initiated cycle. The S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses. The E155K and V137M mutants showed intermediate impairment, and a control variant (V16F) behaved like wildtype. The authors concluded that the assay suggested loss of function.

The variant lies at chr18:11,753,820 (hg19) and is a possible splice site mutation. However, the effect could not be proven because GNAL expression was undetectable in patient lymphoblasts.

checks.evidence_quote: Bioinformatics analysis enumerating all possible splice sites in the human genome suggests that the wild type sequence is 10 times more likely to be found near an acceptor splice site than the mutant sequence.

checks.claim: The splicing effect of the GNAL c.274-5T-C variant could not be proven because GNAL expression was undetectable in patient lymphoblasts.
checks.evidence_quote: we were unable to prove this hypothesis in patient samples, as lymphoblasts are the only tissue available, and GNAL expression is undetectable by semi-quantitative PCR and western blot analysis
